title: The River That Lost Its Voice

pages.text: Years earlier, when twelve-year-old Esi was only in Primary 2, the river beside her town sang a clear, bubbling song over smooth grey pebbles. Silver tilapia darted beneath overhanging fern fronds, and Nana Kwaku’s riverside vegetable beds gleamed green. Now that she was in JHS 1, however, the river had lost its voice. Instead of sparkling over stones, it crept past like thick, yellowish-brown soup.
sentences: Years earlier, when twelve-year-old Esi was only in Primary 2, the river beside her town sang a clear, bubbling song over smooth grey pebbles.
Silver tilapia darted beneath overhanging fern fronds, and Nana Kwaku’s riverside vegetable beds gleamed green.
Now that she was in JHS 1, however, the river had lost its voice.
Instead of sparkling over stones, it crept past like thick, yellowish-brown soup.
pages.alt: Twelve-year-old Esi and her grandfather Nana Kwaku stand on the high bank looking down at a river that has turned thick and muddy yellowish-brown.

pages.text: Esi took a step down the bank with an empty glass jar, hoping to scoop a sample for her school science club. ‘Stop right there, Esi!’ called Nana Kwaku firmly, holding her shoulder back on the dry path. ‘Never touch, wade into, or scoop polluted river water with your bare hands! Upstream, unregulated machines have been digging up the riverbed for gold, galamsey, and only trained scientists in protective gear should collect samples.’
sentences: Esi took a step down the bank with an empty glass jar, hoping to scoop a sample for her school science club.
‘Stop right there, Esi!’ called Nana Kwaku firmly, holding her shoulder back on the dry path.
‘Never touch, wade into, or scoop polluted river water with your bare hands!
Upstream, unregulated machines have been digging up the riverbed for gold, galamsey, and only trained scientists in protective gear should collect samples.’
pages.alt: Nana Kwaku firmly keeps Esi back on the safe dry bank away from the muddy river water.

pages.text: At school the next day, Esi’s science teacher invited Dr Adwoa Mensah, a certified water-quality scientist working with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Water Resources Commission, to visit the town. Wearing thick protective gloves, boots and goggles, Dr Mensah used a long telescopic sampling pole from the bridge to collect river water into sealed laboratory bottles.
sentences: At school the next day, Esi’s science teacher invited Dr Adwoa Mensah, a certified water-quality scientist working with the Environmental Protection Agency and the Water Resources Commission, to visit the town.
Wearing thick protective gloves, boots and goggles, Dr Mensah used a long telescopic sampling pole from the bridge to collect river water into sealed laboratory bottles.
pages.alt: Dr Adwoa Mensah, wearing protective gloves, boots and goggles, uses a long sampling pole from the bridge while Esi and her classmates watch from a safe distance.

pages.text: Back at the school veranda, Dr Mensah held up one sealed transparent bottle of river water beside a bottle of clean tap water. ‘Look at the thick cloudiness in the river bottle,’ she said. ‘Scientists call this high turbidity, caused by suspended sediment, fine clay, silt and sand churned up when excavators strip away riverbank soil and wash gold-bearing gravel directly in the stream.’
sentences: Back at the school veranda, Dr Mensah held up one sealed transparent bottle of river water beside a bottle of clean tap water.
‘Look at the thick cloudiness in the river bottle,’ she said.
‘Scientists call this high turbidity, caused by suspended sediment, fine clay, silt and sand churned up when excavators strip away riverbank soil and wash gold-bearing gravel directly in the stream.’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah holds up a sealed bottle of cloudy brown river water beside a sealed bottle of crystal-clear water.

pages.text: ‘How does suspended sediment harm the river’s living things, even before we talk about chemicals?’ asked Esi. ‘In three ways,’ explained Dr Mensah. ‘First, muddy water blocks sunlight from reaching underwater plants, stopping photosynthesis. Second, heavy silt clogs the delicate gills of fish and smothers fish eggs on the riverbed. Third, it fills up the deep channel, making floods worse during heavy rains!’
sentences: ‘How does suspended sediment harm the river’s living things, even before we talk about chemicals?’ asked Esi.
‘In three ways,’ explained Dr Mensah.
‘First, muddy water blocks sunlight from reaching underwater plants, stopping photosynthesis.
Second, heavy silt clogs the delicate gills of fish and smothers fish eggs on the riverbed.
Third, it fills up the deep channel, making floods worse during heavy rains!’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah shows a diagram of how muddy water blocks sunlight from aquatic plants and clogs fish gills.

pages.text: Then a classmate shouted, ‘I can see mercury in that brown bottle!’ Dr Mensah raised a finger carefully. ‘Let us think like real scientists. Can your eyes see dissolved mercury or heavy metals just by looking at muddy brown water? No! Brown colour proves there is suspended soil and sediment. Confirming whether toxic mercury or arsenic is present requires specialised laboratory instruments.’
sentences: Then a classmate shouted, ‘I can see mercury in that brown bottle!’ Dr Mensah raised a finger carefully.
‘Let us think like real scientists.
Can your eyes see dissolved mercury or heavy metals just by looking at muddy brown water?
No!
Brown colour proves there is suspended soil and sediment.
Confirming whether toxic mercury or arsenic is present requires specialised laboratory instruments.’
pages.alt: Dr Mensah explains the scientific difference between visible mud (turbidity) and invisible chemical contaminants that require laboratory testing.

pages.text: ‘Why do some illegal mining sites use mercury at all?’ asked Esi. ‘In poorly regulated operations,’ said Dr Mensah, ‘mercury is sometimes mixed with crushed ore to bind tiny gold specks into an amalgam, and then burned off. If mercury enters a river, bacteria convert it into methylmercury, which builds up in fish and can severely damage human nerves, kidneys and growing children’s brains.’
sentences: ‘Why do some illegal mining sites use mercury at all?’ asked Esi.
‘In poorly regulated operations,’ said Dr Mensah, ‘mercury is sometimes mixed with crushed ore to bind tiny gold specks into an amalgam, and then burned off.
If mercury enters a river, bacteria convert it into methylmercury, which builds up in fish and can severely damage human nerves, kidneys and growing children’s brains.’
pages.alt: A scientific diagram illustrates how chemical pollutants enter aquatic food chains and why laboratory monitoring protects public health.

pages.text: Next, the class visited the regional water-treatment plant intake with Dr Mensah. The station engineer showed them how extreme turbidity forced the plant to shut down its pumps for hours to protect the machinery, and tripled the amount of alum and treatment chemicals needed to make the water safe for homes and hospitals. Meanwhile, Nana Kwaku could no longer irrigate his vegetables from the stream, and cocoa farms had been dug into open pits.
sentences: Next, the class visited the regional water-treatment plant intake with Dr Mensah.

The station engineer showed them how extreme turbidity forced the plant to shut down its pumps for hours to protect the machinery, and tripled the amount of alum and treatment chemicals needed to make the water safe for homes and hospitals.
Meanwhile, Nana Kwaku could no longer irrigate his vegetables from the stream, and cocoa farms had been dug into open pits.
pages.alt: At a water-treatment plant, an engineer points to clogged intake screens while Dr Mensah, Esi and Nana Kwaku listen.

pages.text: At the town community meeting that Friday, twenty-two-year-old Kojo stood up honestly. ‘I worked at an unregulated pit for six months because I needed money after school,’ Kojo admitted quietly. ‘A middleman took most of the gold money, my friend injured his leg when a pit wall collapsed, and now the very stream my mother drinks from is spoiled. We young people want honest work that does not destroy our home!’
sentences: At the town community meeting that Friday, twenty-two-year-old Kojo stood up honestly.
‘I worked at an unregulated pit for six months because I needed money after school,’ Kojo admitted quietly.
‘A middleman took most of the gold money, my friend injured his leg when a pit wall collapsed, and now the very stream my mother drinks from is spoiled.
We young people want honest work that does not destroy our home!’
pages.alt: At a town meeting, young Kojo speaks honestly to elders, farmers and Dr Mensah about why youth need safe, lawful livelihoods.

pages.text: One week later, Dr Mensah returned with the official certified laboratory report from Accra. The lab tests confirmed both dangerous turbidity and elevated mercury levels downstream of the illegal pits, providing verified legal evidence! The community elders, the District Assembly and the Water Resources Commission used that report to halt the illegal dredging and launch a licensed land-reclamation project.
sentences: One week later, Dr Mensah returned with the official certified laboratory report from Accra.
The lab tests confirmed both dangerous turbidity and elevated mercury levels downstream of the illegal pits, providing verified legal evidence!
The community elders, the District Assembly and the Water Resources Commission used that report to halt the illegal dredging and launch a licensed land-reclamation project.
pages.alt: Dr Mensah presents the official laboratory report to the town elders and District Assembly officers.

pages.text: Kojo and thirty young men and women joined a paid reclamation and agro-forestry cooperative. Trained by engineers and agronomists, they backfilled dangerous open pits with rock and subsoil, spread rich compost, and planted fast-growing bamboo, oil palm and native riverbank trees whose roots hold soil in place and filter runoff naturally.
sentences: Kojo and thirty young men and women joined a paid reclamation and agro-forestry cooperative.

Trained by engineers and agronomists, they backfilled dangerous open pits with rock and subsoil, spread rich compost, and planted fast-growing bamboo, oil palm and native riverbank trees whose roots hold soil in place and filter runoff naturally.
pages.alt: Kojo and young adult workers in safety boots refill old pits and plant bamboo and native trees along the riverbank buffer zone.

pages.text: Eighteen months later, Esi stood with Nana Kwaku and Dr Mensah on the bridge. The river was not completely healed overnight, restoring an ecosystem takes years of vigilance, but the water ran clearer, green reeds lined the banks, and tiny fingerlings darted in the shallows again. ‘A river cannot speak in court or parliament,’ Esi wrote in her notebook, ‘so science, law and caring citizens must be its voice.’
sentences: Eighteen months later, Esi stood with Nana Kwaku and Dr Mensah on the bridge.

The river was not completely healed overnight, restoring an ecosystem takes years of vigilance, but the water ran clearer, green reeds lined the banks, and tiny fingerlings darted in the shallows again.
‘A river cannot speak in court or parliament,’ Esi wrote in her notebook, ‘so science, law and caring citizens must be its voice.’
pages.alt: Standing on the bridge eighteen months later, Esi, Nana Kwaku, Kojo and Dr Mensah look down at a much clearer stream lined with young green bamboo and trees.

activities.question: Why did Nana Kwaku stop Esi from scooping the muddy river water with her own jar?
options: Polluted water is unsafe; only trained scientists in gear sample it
Glass jars melt instantaneously when they touch river water
Nana Kwaku wanted to drink the muddy water himself
activities.explanation: Children must never touch, wade into, or sample polluted water; certified scientists use protective equipment and sampling poles.

activities.definition: Cloudiness in water caused by suspended particles of soil, silt and clay
distractors: The speed of wind blowing over a mountain
A certificate given to cocoa farmers

activities.question: Why could the students NOT prove mercury was in the bottle just by looking at the brown colour?
options: Brown shows mud; dissolved heavy metals require lab tests to confirm
Mercury turns river water bright purple with yellow stars
Mercury only exists on other planets
activities.explanation: Visual observation only shows turbidity (suspended sediment); identifying chemical contaminants like mercury requires certified laboratory analysis.

activities.question: How did the town address both the environmental damage and the youth unemployment problem?
options: By stopping illegal mining and employing youth to reclaim the land
By paving over the entire river with concrete
By asking Primary 6 pupils to dig the pits by hand
activities.explanation: Lawful enforcement paired with paid land reclamation, bamboo buffer planting and agro-forestry created safe livelihoods while healing the land.

activities.prompt: Order the steps that helped protect and begin healing the river.
items: Stay safely away from polluted water and alert certified scientists.
Test water samples in a laboratory to confirm sediment and chemical levels.
Enforce environmental laws and employ youth to reclaim land and plant buffers.

activities.prompt: How did listening to both Dr Mensah’s scientific evidence and Kojo’s honest story help the community find a lasting solution?

glossary.definition: The cloudiness or haziness of water caused by suspended soil, silt and clay particles
Solid particles of soil, sand and silt carried in water or settled on a riverbed
The process by which green plants use sunlight to make food and release oxygen
A toxic heavy metal that can poison water, fish and human nervous systems if released during mining
Restoring damaged, mined land by refilling pits, rebuilding soil and planting vegetation
